title: NIMS Hyderabad reduces deep brain stimulation surgery time with new technique
summary: Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS), Hyderabad, has introduced a technique that reduces deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery time from 5–6 hours to 1–2 hours in select patients by using advanced imaging, precise surgical planning and refined operative methods allowing general anaesthesia. NIMS also offers MRI-guided radiofrequency ablation for medication-refractory tremors and provides free treatment to eligible patients through relief funds.
content:
Updated- July 26, 2026 10:15 pm IST - HYDERABAD

The Department of Neurosurgery at Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS), Hyderabad, has introduced an advanced technique that reduces the duration of Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) surgery from the conventional 5-6 hours to just 1-2 hours in select patients.

According to NIMS, the procedure was implemented by Y. Vamsi Krishna, head of the Department of Neurosurgery. The institute said the technique combines advanced imaging, precise surgical planning and refined operative methods, enabling DBS procedures to be performed under general anaesthesia instead of the conventional awake craniotomy approach.

DBS is used to treat movement disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, essential tremor and dystonia. Traditionally, patients undergoing the surgery are required to remain awake for several hours while electrodes are implanted in specific areas of the brain. The new approach aims to reduce patient discomfort and operative time while maintaining the accuracy of electrode placement.

The institute said the neurosurgery team adopted the technique after receiving specialised training at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, University College London. NIMS added that more than 200 DBS surgeries have been performed at the institute over the past two-and-a-half years, indicating growing local expertise in functional neurosurgery.

In a related development, NIMS has introduced MRI-guided radiofrequency ablation for patients with tremors that do not respond to medication. The procedure uses advanced MRI sequences to identify and target the dentato-rubro-thalamic (DRT) pathway accurately and does not require implantation of any permanent device. This offers a less invasive alternative for selected patients with disabling tremor.

The institute noted that while similar procedures can cost around ₹5 lakh in private hospitals, qualifying underprivileged patients can receive the treatment free of cost through the Chief Minister’s Relief Fund. The move is expected to improve access to advanced neurosurgical care for socioeconomically disadvantaged groups.
